question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, because a polygenic score is built from a finite set of SNPs that reach genome-wide significance in a GWAS, so by construction it omits the many small-effect variants that still contribute to total SNP heritability; the variance it explains is therefore necessarily a strict subset of SNP h².

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Observing the question and options for now without committing to an answer yet, as more discussion might clarify edge cases around measurement and SNP coverage.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total additive variance tagged by the measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on variance that any linear combination of those SNPs can explain). A polygenic score is simply one particular linear combination of the SNPs. With infinite training-sample size, perfect LD information, and inclusion of every causal variant, the PGS weights converge to the true causal effects and the out-of-sample \(R^2\) therefore converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Consequently the PGS \(R^2\) is bounded above by, but is not required to be strictly below, SNP heritability; the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance captured by the additive effects of all measured SNPs (i.e., \(\mathrm{Var}(X\beta)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)\)). A polygenic score constructed with the exact, population-level SNP effect sizes \(\beta\) therefore explains precisely \(h^2_{SNP}\) of the variance; equality is attainable in the theoretical limit of infinite data and perfect effect-size knowledge. Because the statement claims the PGS \(R^2\) is “necessarily” (i.e., always strictly) lower, the claim is false.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The predictive ability of a polygenic score (typically measured as R² in an independent sample) is necessarily lower than SNP heritability because the score is constructed from a finite set of estimated SNP effects that are subject to winner's curse, incomplete tagging, and LD pruning. Even when using all SNPs below a liberal p-value threshold, the realized variance explained falls short of the theoretical SNP-h² ceiling estimated by methods like GCTA or LD score regression, which assume perfect knowledge of the causal effects. Papers I've seen consistently report PGS R² values well below the corresponding SNP-h² estimates for the same trait, confirming this gap is structural rather than merely technical.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that would be captured by the *true* (unknown) effects of all SNPs jointly. A polygenic score is a linear predictor whose weights are *estimated* from finite data; the resulting out-of-sample \(R^2\) is therefore attenuated by estimation error, winner’s-curse effects, imperfect LD tagging, and any additional shrinkage or pruning that is applied. Consequently the attainable \(R^2\) is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) for any finite sample, so the inequality holds by necessity.

(The equality is recovered only in the theoretical limit \(N\to\infty\), which is outside the scope of any actual polygenic score.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is in principle capturable by the additive effects of all measured (or imputed) SNPs. A polygenic score \(\hat{G}\) is an estimator of the latent genetic value \(G\) that underlies \(h^2_{SNP}\). Because effect-size estimates are obtained from finite samples, they contain noise; the out-of-sample correlation \(\text{Corr}(Y,\hat{G})\) is therefore attenuated relative to \(\text{Corr}(Y,G)\). Consequently, the variance explained by any realizable PGS is strictly bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, in finite data, is necessarily lower. Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples would equality be achieved—an unattainable condition for any practical polygenic score.
